title: Sizing London's market for electric cargo bikes
prompt: Tandrel, a European maker of electric cargo bikes, is thinking about opening a sales and service centre in London aimed at delivery businesses. Before it decides, it wants to know how big the opportunity is. Estimate the yearly market, in pounds, for new electric cargo bikes bought by delivery businesses in London, and tell the client whether it is big enough.

facts.answer: Tandrel makes electric cargo bikes and sells them in several European cities. It would open a London sales and service centre only if it could expect at least £2 million of bike sales a year there, the level at which its centres in other cities cover their running costs.

New electric cargo bikes bought each year by businesses that deliver goods in Greater London, valued at the price paid. Count a leased bike once, at its purchase price. Leave out servicing, spare batteries, insurance and riders' pay.

Three groups: parcel carriers, grocery and meal-kit delivery firms, and local businesses that deliver their own goods, such as pharmacies, florists and print shops. A table of deliveries by segment is available.
Leave them out. Takeaway riders mostly use their own bikes, e-bikes or mopeds, not cargo bikes, and the delivery businesses do not buy them.
Estimate next year's market, starting from the bikes working in London today.
Ignore spares. Assume every bike in the fleet works every delivery day, and that the table shows a typical delivery day.
Assume a cargo bike in daily delivery use lasts about 4 years before it is replaced.
For simplicity, assume the bikes' ages are spread evenly, so about one in four wears out each year.
Assume the number of electric cargo bikes working for London delivery businesses grows by 25% next year, as more businesses swap vans for bikes in central areas.
Assume an average price of £6,000 per bike, including the cargo box and battery, after fleet discounts.

Once its centre is running, Tandrel expects to win about 20% of the market, similar to its share in other cities where it has a service centre. In those cities it reached that share in the centre's second year.
Assume a handful of other makers sell cargo bikes in London, mostly through general bike shops, and that none runs a sales and service centre just for delivery businesses.
Ignore them. Delivery businesses almost always buy new bikes so that they get the warranty and servicing.

key_buckets: Define the market: new bikes bought per year, in pounds, by delivery businesses in London
Segment the users: parcel carriers, grocery and meal kits, local businesses
Working fleet per segment: deliveries made by bike divided by deliveries per bike per day
Yearly purchases: replacing worn-out bikes plus growth of the fleet
Value and the client's question: bikes times price, then Tandrel's share against its £2 million bar
good_signs: Separates the number of bikes in use (the fleet) from the number bought each year
Segments by type of delivery business rather than starting from London's population
States each assumption clearly and rounds to keep the maths simple
Asks what bar the client uses to decide, before sizing anything
Sense-checks the result and names the assumption that matters most
red_flags: Treats the whole fleet as if it were bought every year
Counts takeaway riders' own bikes or e-bikes
Gives a market size without answering whether it is big enough for the client

exhibits.title: Deliveries in London per day, by segment (case assumptions)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask how many deliveries each segment makes, how many are made by cargo bike, and how many deliveries one bike makes in a day.
exhibits.insight: The working fleet is about 5,000 bikes: 1,500 for parcels, 1,500 for groceries and meal kits, and 2,000 for local businesses. Parcel carriers make 75% of deliveries but need only 30% of the bikes, because only 6% of parcels go by bike and one parcel bike makes 60 drops a day; local businesses make 10% of deliveries but need 40% of the bikes. Local businesses and grocery firms together run 70% of the bikes.

math.question: How many electric cargo bikes are working for delivery businesses in London today?
math.expression: parcel_deliveries * parcel_bike_pct / 100 / parcel_per_bike + grocery_deliveries * grocery_bike_pct / 100 / grocery_per_bike + local_deliveries * local_bike_pct / 100 / local_per_bike
math.working: Parcels: 1,500,000 x 6% = 90,000 bike deliveries a day, / 60 per bike = 1,500 bikes. Groceries and meal kits: 300,000 x 10% = 30,000, / 20 = 1,500 bikes. Local businesses: 200,000 x 10% = 20,000, / 10 = 2,000 bikes. Total 5,000 bikes.

math.question: How many new electric cargo bikes will London delivery businesses buy next year?
math.working: Replacements: 5,000 bikes / 4-year life = 1,250 a year. Growth: 25% of 5,000 = 1,250 extra bikes. Total 2,500 new bikes, half of them from growth.

math.question: What is the market worth next year, in £ million?
math.working: 2,500 bikes x £6,000 = £15,000,000, which is £15 million a year.

math.question: If Tandrel wins 20% of the market, how much would it sell in London a year, in £ million?
math.working: 20% of £15 million is £3 million a year, 50% above Tandrel's £2 million bar. Put the other way, Tandrel needs about 13% of a £15 million market (2 / 15) to reach its bar.

math.question: Keeping the 20% share and the £6,000 price, what is the lowest fleet growth next year, as a percentage, at which Tandrel would still reach its £2 million bar?
math.working: To sell £2 million at a 20% share, the market must be £10 million (2 / 20%). At £6,000 a bike that is about 1,667 bikes. Replacements give 1,250, so growth must add about 417 bikes, about 8% of the 5,000 fleet. The case assumes 25%, so growth could fall by about two-thirds before Tandrel misses its bar.

brainstorm.question: What could make this market, or Tandrel's share of it, bigger or smaller than your estimate over the next few years?
idea_bank: Tighter low-emission or congestion charges that push more businesses out of vans and onto bikes
More micro-hubs (small depots in central areas) that make short bike rounds possible
Cargo-bike parking and loading bays on busy streets, or a lack of them
Electric vans getting cheaper, which removes the emissions reason to switch to bikes
Longer-lasting bikes and batteries, which lower the number of replacements
Theft and insurance costs putting smaller businesses off
Leasing and rental schemes making bikes affordable for small local businesses
A shortage of riders, or rising riders' pay
Growth slowing once the easy central routes have switched, which would cut the growth half of yearly purchases
Large parcel carriers buying through Europe-wide fleet deals rather than from a London centre, which would cut Tandrel's share of that segment
Small local businesses, which have no workshop of their own, valuing a nearby service centre most, which would help Tandrel's share
Other makers opening their own centres for delivery businesses once Tandrel shows there is demand

must_mention: A market of about £15 million a year: about 2,500 new bikes at £6,000, from a working fleet of about 5,000
At a 20% share Tandrel would sell about £3 million a year, above its £2 million bar
Half of next year's purchases come from fleet growth, so the answer depends most on growth continuing
good_signs: Gives a range, for example £12 million to £18 million

Shows how much room there is: fleet growth could fall from 25% to about 8% before Tandrel misses its bar, and with no growth at all the market is about £7.5 million and Tandrel's sales about £1.5 million
Notes that Tandrel needs about 13% of the market to reach £2 million, and that its share takes about two years to build, so the first year will be lower
Says which customers to target first: local businesses and grocery firms run 70% of the bikes and are the most likely to value a nearby service centre
Notes that a fast-growing fleet is young, so fewer bikes may need replacing next year than fleet divided by life suggests
Suggests how to check the numbers, such as asking large parcel carriers about their bike plans

model_answer_outline: Clarify: next year's spending on new electric cargo bikes by London delivery businesses, valued at the price paid, with leased bikes counted once and takeaway riders' own bikes left out. Tandrel needs £2 million of yearly sales for a centre to cover its costs.
Structure: working fleet by segment, then yearly purchases (replacements plus growth), then value, then Tandrel's share against its bar.

Fleet: parcels 1,500,000 deliveries a day x 6% by bike / 60 per bike = 1,500; groceries and meal kits 300,000 x 10% / 20 = 1,500; local businesses 200,000 x 10% / 10 = 2,000. About 5,000 bikes in total, 70% of them with grocery firms and local businesses.
Purchases: 5,000 / 4-year life = 1,250 replacements, plus 25% growth = 1,250 extra bikes. About 2,500 bikes a year.
Value: 2,500 x £6,000 = about £15 million a year. At a 20% share Tandrel would sell about £3 million, 50% above its bar.

Sense-check and risk: half the purchases come from growth. Growth could fall from 25% to about 8% before a 20% share drops below £2 million; with no growth at all the market halves to £7.5 million and Tandrel would sell about £1.5 million. Tandrel needs about 13% of the market, and its share takes about two years to build.

Recommendation: yes, the market is big enough, so open the centre, but start lean (for example a service point shared with a partner). Lead with local businesses and grocery firms, which run most of the bikes and most need nearby servicing, and expand once the large parcel carriers confirm their fleet plans.
